speakers: Katie Kaminski (Alpha Simplex, trend following researcher)
Harry Moore (partner and senior client portfolio manager, Man AHL)
summary: Systematic Investor episode on Q1 2026 trend following performance (March pivot to inflation and energy) and four papers: optimal market mix for trend, portable alpha, trend drawdowns, assessing alpha in macro strategies. Conclusions: trend diversified in March; traditional liquid markets give crisis alpha; drawdowns are normal.

coverage.note: Intro and small talk; nothing actionable
Small talk; Q1 2026 headlines; trend vs equities
Q1 2026 trend review: pivot to inflation, YTD numbers
March dispersion; speed; pure trend vs mixed
Differentiators; March positioning; carry; index results
March index returns; optimal market mix paper intro
Market mix paper: macro factors, crisis vs long-run Sharpe, cash efficiency
Trend and macro themes; crisis alpha criteria
Cash buffers; trend margin in crisis
Simulation of 0.6 Sharpe drawdown; Liberation Day shock
Drawdowns self-correct; change; probability of drawdowns

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: gold the the deepest or the steepest drop on a monthly basis, I think, since the autumn of 2008.
claims.claim: In March 2026 the S&P had its worst quarter since 2022, gold its steepest monthly drop since autumn 2008 and the 60/40 portfolio was stress-tested, a regime in which stocks, bonds and gold fell together.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: this is the sixth or seventh month in a row where trend following uh measured by the SocGen Trend Index has outperformed the MSCI World Index.
claims.claim: Trend following (SocGen Trend Index) has outperformed MSCI World for six or seven consecutive months into March 2026.
claims.indicator: SocGen Trend Index vs MSCI World

claims.speaker: Katie Kaminski
claims.quote: you kind of found that new trends were building as other trends were pivoting.
claims.claim: In Q1 2026 trend followers profited in January and February from continuing themes (weaker dollar, strong equities); in March the themes flipped (inflation, huge energy move), and new trends offset reversals of old ones.
claims.direction: long energy, short bonds in March; long equities and short dollar before
claims.conditions: Works when new trends form quickly enough to offset reversals
claims.testable: yes - trend index returns by sector

claims.speaker: Katie Kaminski
claims.quote: that diversification that energies and other asset classes, like some of the short rate positions or short positions in fixed income, that profited from the inflation concerns
claims.claim: Energy and short fixed-income/rate positions profited from inflation worries and offset equity losses, showing the diversification value of trend.
claims.indicator: energy and short bond trend positions
claims.direction: long energy and short bonds in inflation shocks

claims.speaker: Harry Moore
claims.quote: between 3 and kind of 7% on a year-to-date basis
claims.claim: Most trend index formulations were up roughly 3 to 7% year to date at end of Q1 2026, a good result against equities, bonds and 60/40.

claims.speaker: Harry Moore
claims.quote: And it doesn't seem to be equities. It certainly doesn't seem to be bonds.
claims.claim: If inflation returns or escalation continues, neither equities, bonds, gold (wobbling) nor private markets help; trend is a candidate defensive allocation.
claims.indicator: trend vs equities, bonds, gold in inflationary stress
claims.conditions: Applies to an inflationary or escalation scenario

claims.speaker: Katie Kaminski
claims.quote: how much energy you had was sort of PCA one, right? So, the more energy you had, the better things were.
claims.claim: March 2026 dispersion among trend managers came mostly from energy exposure (the first principal component) and from avoiding positions that were selling off.
claims.indicator: energy exposure as PC1 of March dispersion

claims.speaker: Katie Kaminski
claims.quote: speed was helpful. So, being able to pivot out of some of these you know, reversing trends also helped.
claims.claim: Faster trend models did better in March 2026 because they could pivot out of reversing trends.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: I certainly get the suspicion that certainly not all of them are pure trend anymore.
claims.claim: Large CTAs are not pure trend any more; carry and value sub-strategies may explain a good March, so trend should be compared like for like.

claims.speaker: Harry Moore
claims.quote: I think once you go below 80, 70% trend following, right? You're starting to introduce different return drivers.
claims.claim: Below 70 to 80% trend content, a manager has other return drivers, so a dedicated trend mandate should be judged for how its non-trend part behaves.

claims.speaker: Harry Moore
claims.quote: if I'm looking at something that I I would call trend following, I want that to be a divergent strategy.
claims.claim: Trend following should be a divergent strategy, continuing to bet on what is happening, as opposed to convergent strategies.

claims.speaker: Harry Moore
claims.quote: if there's a kind of full liquidity break, a dash for cash, sometimes they have these these kind of horrible left tails.
claims.claim: Carry, value and similar strategies may do well in a mid-distribution equity unwind but can show horrible left tails in a full liquidity break.
claims.indicator: carry and value in liquidity crises

claims.speaker: Katie Kaminski
claims.quote: I often just point to the three key differentiators. One is speed, one is market set, third is like trend or non-trend, so how much non-trend.
claims.claim: Manager performance differences come from speed, market set and trend vs non-trend share.

claims.speaker: Harry Moore
claims.quote: if you were already long oil coming into March, then you should have done had some some good offsetting profits there.
claims.claim: Positioning into March: long oil helped, bonds were mixed because fast models were long then switched short, and most were long equities then scaled down as momentum flipped.

claims.speaker: Katie Kaminski
claims.quote: energy carry worked very well. Um FX carry worked well. Bond carry didn't work so well.
claims.claim: In March 2026 energy carry and FX carry worked while bond carry did not.

claims.speaker: Katie Kaminski
claims.quote: we did see that faster was good except for maybe in fixed income.
claims.claim: Faster trend worked in March except in fixed income, which has been a headache for over a year because pivots keep failing.
claims.indicator: speed of trend in fixed income

claims.speaker: Katie Kaminski
claims.quote: when you have the key strongest trend and you have a 50% move in energy, like every different, you know, if you're 10% or if you're 20%, like that makes a huge difference.
claims.claim: Market-set weights matter when one sector makes a huge move (50% in energy): 10% vs 20% energy weight changes results greatly.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: The Beta 50 Index looks to be down only 1.44% still up 7.15% for the year.
claims.claim: Trend indices (Beta 50, SocGen CTA, SocGen Trend) fell only about 0.7 to 1.5% in March 2026 and were up 7% or more YTD.
claims.indicator: Beta 50, SocGen CTA and Trend indices

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: And the S&P 500 Total Return Index down almost 5% in March, down 4.33% so relatively speaking
claims.claim: Against the S&P (down about 4.3% YTD), MSCI World and world government bonds, trend did well in March, answering critics who said there was no crisis alpha; the short-term traders index did best (+56 bp).
claims.indicator: trend indices vs S&P, MSCI World, bonds

claims.speaker: Harry Moore
claims.quote: if you trade more quickly you tend to have more crisis alpha if you tend if you trade more a little bit slower you tend to have a slightly higher sharp.
claims.claim: Faster trend trading gives more crisis alpha while slower trading gives a slightly higher Sharpe.
claims.direction: fast for crisis alpha, slow for Sharpe

claims.speaker: Harry Moore
claims.quote: things like Nordic hydropower it might be iron ore.
claims.claim: The market universe can be widened from traditional cleared futures (crude, gold) to alternative markets (Nordic hydropower, iron ore, Chinese bitumen and glass) and synthetic markets (equity factors) with different return drivers.

claims.speaker: Harry Moore
claims.quote: using essentially a maximum diversification so you're you're you're not putting too much weight into into any individual market
claims.claim: The paper builds portfolios with maximum diversification so no market dominates.

claims.speaker: Harry Moore
claims.quote: you say hey well the traditional markets they tended to give me my best sharp in the crisis periods whereas my alternative markets have tended to give me a higher sharp ratio over the long run.
claims.claim: Traditional markets gave the best Sharpe in crises while alternative markets gave a higher long-run Sharpe.

claims.speaker: Harry Moore
claims.quote: the traditional markets tend to pick up more of those macro factors. And the alternative markets tend to pick up less and so they have more idiosyncratic return drivers.
claims.claim: Traditional markets load more on macro factors (risk on/off, growth, inflation, monetary policy) while alternative markets have more idiosyncratic drivers.

claims.speaker: Harry Moore
claims.quote: in these in these sell-offs things like risk on risk off or inflation they explain more and therefore the traditional markets do better.
claims.claim: In sell-offs macro factors explain more variance (principal components), so traditional markets do better then.
claims.indicator: macro factor variance share in sell-offs

claims.speaker: Harry Moore
claims.quote: that maximum crisis sharp overweights traditional markets.
claims.claim: Maximum crisis-Sharpe portfolio overweights gold, crude and dollar-vs-pound; maximum long-run-Sharpe portfolio overweights alternative markets (hydropower, iron ore, China commodities).

claims.speaker: Harry Moore
claims.quote: traditional markets are great for that that cash efficiency.
claims.claim: Traditional markets give maximum cash efficiency, so for portable alpha a trend allocation needs little cash.

claims.speaker: Harry Moore
claims.quote: if I trade value in the US and I trade value in Japan and I trade value in Europe like those aren't perfectly correlated.
claims.claim: About 60 equity factors come from roughly 15 style factors times four regions, since regional versions are imperfectly correlated and count as separate markets (about 900 markets overall).

claims.speaker: Harry Moore
claims.quote: If I trade 30 commodity markets cocoa gold crude right? They're they're they're less correlated.
claims.claim: Number of markets is a poor measure of diversification: 30 stock indices are highly correlated while 30 commodities are not.

claims.speaker: Katie Kaminski
claims.quote: given the markets that we can trade, what are the different objective functions and what should investors do given those different objective functions?
claims.claim: Optimal market mix depends on the objective: max standalone Sharpe vs a defensive crisis-alpha add-on.

claims.speaker: Katie Kaminski
claims.quote: for those investors out there looking at risk mitigation, they're actually sort of close to their cash optimal portfolio as well.
claims.claim: The crisis-alpha portfolio and cash-efficient portfolio are similar, so risk mitigators also get cash efficiency.

claims.speaker: Katie Kaminski
claims.quote: with trend, you actually are following a lot of the big macro themes and capturing them with a process that's diligent and sort of systematic as opposed to trying to predict which macro theme is going to occur and when.
claims.claim: Trend gives exposure to macro themes without needing a forecast of which theme or when.

claims.speaker: Katie Kaminski
claims.quote: it's a few key things. One, being unbiased. You know, two, being liquid. Three, being adaptable.
claims.claim: Crisis alpha needs a strategy to be unbiased, liquid and adaptable.

claims.speaker: Katie Kaminski
claims.quote: it's the things that are liquid that move with the macro themes that have the potential to find opportunities if you can adapt with them quickly enough in markets that are tradeable enough
claims.claim: In a crisis the liquid markets move with macro themes, so liquid traditional markets provide the offsetting returns for a crisis allocation.

claims.speaker: Harry Moore
claims.quote: the kind of evaporation of alpha in active equities.
claims.claim: Alpha evaporation in active equities shifted investors to passive, so portable alpha splits the decision: own the index via swap or future and separately find a repeatable alpha.

claims.speaker: Harry Moore
claims.quote: I'm going to decouple my investment choice. So, the index is hard to beat. Well, why don't I just go and replicate the index?
claims.claim: Portable alpha replicates the index with swaps or futures and layers a separate alpha on top.

claims.speaker: Harry Moore
claims.quote: I don't need $100 to get $100 of trend exposure. I might only need $25 or $30.
claims.claim: Trend uses little cash ($25 to $30 per $100 of exposure), leaving cash to hold the beta index.

claims.speaker: Harry Moore
claims.quote: you are able to to outperform with more consistency.
claims.claim: Historically, trend on top of beta outperformed with more consistency than a multi-strategy alpha.

claims.speaker: Katie Kaminski
claims.quote: adding trend with um as sort of your portable alpha strategy did have the better drawdown characteristic compared to say more equity focused or hedge funds
claims.claim: Trend as portable alpha had better drawdown characteristics than equity-focused or hedge fund alpha.

claims.speaker: Katie Kaminski
claims.quote: alpha and beta are never 100% separated.
claims.claim: Alpha and beta are never fully separated; in March 2026 equities and trend were in drawdown at the same time, as in return-stacked ETFs.
claims.indicator: correlation of alpha and beta in drawdowns

claims.speaker: Harry Moore
claims.quote: those risks from 2008 that caused so many issues, they haven't gone away.
claims.claim: Coincident alpha and beta drawdowns (COVID, GFC) could hurt portable alpha, so structures need due diligence.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: I imagine that there are certain kinds of trend following that probably are better suited for this uh particular uh thing.
claims.claim: Some trend styles (liquid markets, certain speeds) may suit portable alpha better; untested.

claims.speaker: Harry Moore
claims.quote: if the S&P draws down 8, 9, especially if it draws down 10, right? All of your margin is going to be exhausted.
claims.claim: With 10% margin on S&P futures, an 8 to 10% fall exhausts margin, so keep large cash buffers (e.g. $40 per $100 rather than $10) instead of investing the rest.

claims.speaker: Harry Moore
claims.quote: if your alpha isn't liquid, you're not going to be able to source that from your alpha and you'll get closed out of your of your beta.
claims.claim: An illiquid alpha cannot meet margin calls, forcing closure of the beta, so use liquid alpha such as trend.

claims.speaker: Harry Moore
claims.quote: our margin requirements actually go down in the crisis.
claims.claim: Trend manages to risk, so in a crisis its exposure and margin fall, reducing funding needs.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: the industry were in the fifth consecutive months of drawdowns.
claims.claim: By June 2025, after five months of drawdown, SocGen Trend neared its historical maximum drawdown (about 22%) amid the tariff reversals and headlines that trend was too slow for social-media-driven news; a strong recovery followed.

claims.speaker: Harry Moore
claims.quote: then what you should actually do is rebalance in that time.
claims.claim: If an asset's drawdown does not change your belief it no longer works, rebalance into it rather than dropping it.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: trend following for sure would be too slow to deal with a world where political news were communicated through social media
claims.claim: The narrative that trend is too slow for social-media news was refuted by later recovery.

claims.speaker: Harry Moore
claims.quote: Now, that strategy spent years in drawdown. It had a drawdown of 33%.
claims.claim: Simulation: a 0.6 Sharpe strategy at 15% vol (vs equities about 0.4 Sharpe) still had a 33% drawdown lasting years, so a long drawdown does not show a broken strategy.

claims.speaker: Harry Moore
claims.quote: what about if you set drawdown rules such that you deallocate from strategies um when they have drawdowns, and and again you find um that underperforms.
claims.claim: Rules that deallocate from strategies in drawdown underperform holding.

claims.speaker: Harry Moore
claims.quote: There's a lot of well-documented biases from humans psychology that explain um why trend following works over the long run.
claims.claim: Human behavioural biases explain why trend works over the long run.

claims.speaker: Katie Kaminski
claims.quote: that type of shock is very difficult for trend because there's no actual trend yet.
claims.claim: A sudden shock such as Liberation Day is hard for trend because there is no trend yet, only confusion about the macro meaning.

claims.speaker: Katie Kaminski
claims.quote: of macro change takes time. It takes time for tariffs to affect prices.
claims.claim: Realisation of macro change takes time (tariffs to prices), and trends return afterwards.

claims.speaker: Katie Kaminski
claims.quote: over time the strategy is sort of self-correcting, just like most strategies
claims.claim: Trend drawdowns are cyclical and self-correcting, as in the 2013 CTA winter and the second-largest drawdown since 2000.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: Change will hit all strategies that have a conversion profile because they don't like change.
claims.claim: Change hurts convergent strategies while divergent strategies such as trend are designed for it.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: But if you've been around for 25 years, like some of us have, that number goes to almost 80%.
claims.claim: The probability of a two-standard-deviation drawdown is about 21% after five years but almost 80% over 25 years for a 0.5 Sharpe, 10% vol strategy, so a short clean record is weak evidence.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: dropping from somewhere almost 30% back in the late '90s to now it's just 5% of the total hedge fund universe
claims.claim: CTA AUM fell from almost 30% of hedge fund AUM to 5% and to about 2% of futures volume, so crowding is not a credible reason for trend to fail.
claims.indicator: CTA AUM share of hedge funds and futures volume

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: I think the real question is did people change?
claims.claim: Trends form because human behaviour does not change; the world changing does not break trend.

claims.speaker: Katie Kaminski
claims.quote: we kind of showed mathematically how you can tease out sort of take out the equity and trend exposure and understand the idiosyncratic alpha that you have in a particular manager.
claims.claim: Remove equity and trend exposures from macro managers' returns to measure idiosyncratic alpha.
claims.indicator: macro manager alpha vs equity and trend

claims.speaker: Harry Moore
claims.quote: Now, there's a very very weak positive correlation between higher fee and higher net of returns from the paper, but it's very weak.
claims.claim: Across macro managers, higher fees are only very weakly related to higher net returns.

claims.speaker: Harry Moore
claims.quote: Uh but the 10 that did badly don't exist anymore. So my data set is very biased towards the the better performers.
claims.claim: Survivorship bias makes current manager indices look better; analysis should account for it.

claims.speaker: Harry Moore
claims.quote: if I can go and access trend via a low cost route and I can access equities through a low cost route. Like what is the actual alpha on top of that.
claims.claim: Decompose macro managers against equities and trend (and bonds) and judge the alpha above cheap trend and equity exposure.

claims.speaker: Katie Kaminski
claims.quote: oil shocks cause a weak in consumer, they also cause inflation shocks.
claims.claim: Oil shocks weaken the consumer and create inflation shocks, so geopolitical risk transmits to managed futures through energy.

claims.speaker: Harry Moore
claims.quote: if we continue to see the inflation theme, I think we'll see yeah, a bit more bit more oil in there. We'll see short bonds.
claims.claim: If the inflation theme continues, trend will be long oil and short bonds.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: I'm not so sure that there is enough people who are well prepared for whatever comes because I still think that the allocation to our space is way too small
claims.claim: Allocations to trend and non-correlated strategies are too small for the risks in 2026 (recovery or deeper crisis).
